doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Petrillo abolishes subsidiaries; Local 669 and the 1960 merger
summary: Local 669 is chartered, a merger is voted down and finally achieved in 1960; he serves on committees and then the Oakland office.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: So when this thing happened with the union, it was in ’46 was it?

Our merger. Yeah we merged. Now I drifted once again. I first started out talking about the black local and I told you the story about the merger, and then I joined in ’37 in a Subsidiary. Well as I think I mentioned before, in ’45 or around the mid-forties, Petrillo abolished the subsidiary locals. Because you had Subsidiary locals all throughout the United States. You had also black chartered locals and they had charters that went back to the early 1900’s and some even the late 1800’s in Chicago, 10-208, so I guess 208 was the black local. See when they merged many of them took the dual numbers. Like 10- 208, that’s the merger. They merged. But anyhow Petrillo abolished the subsidiaries and then as I mentioned before the Federation then gave the locals the choice of accepting the

subsidiaries as full members. Parent local they called it, or failing that, why that’s how we came to have the charter of 669. So in 669 we set up, had our offices, we had a President, we had the Secretary/Treasurer/Business Agent and we had another office secretary and we had a Board of Directors. And I was on the Board of Directors. I got elected to the Board of Directors. And so we asked them on numerous occasions about amalgamation merger. Even one time we got it on the ballot through white friends. But it was defeated. So then as I said before the State of California, it’s in the documentation I’m going to give you. And so anyhow after we merged Pop Kennedy was President at the time. And that was in 1960. And Pop Kennedy, he then proceeded to try to accommodate us as best he could considering that there was resentment from the hard core. So he appointed me to committees. I was on the Wage Scale Committee, I was on the Music Performance Trust Fund Committee. For five years I served on committees. Then an opening occurred in the Oakland branch office. They had this branch office that had been over there I guess since the earthquake. And so he put me in there and that’s when I got my taste of musical bureaucracy. And by then too, your rock bands were really starting to flourish, in the mid-sixties. They were really starting to flourish. And over there then we had clubs opening up over there in Oakland. They would have these rock bands with all that noise. We’d be playing at the Claremont Hotel. That was during the same time I was working at the union. We’d be working in the lounge. Up over the lounge was what they called the Terrace Room. So they’d rent out the Terrace Room to a prom. The Terrace Room accommodated about 800 people. And we’re down below here in the lounge. All of a sudden, crash, bam, thump thump. Noise. And the waitresses would go up and ask them could they please be quiet because they’re disturbing the patrons below. And these kids, being kids, “Oh, we can’t feel it if we don’t play loud.” So it was just terrible. But anyhow what happened, getting back to the union situation, so I worked in the Oakland office and then I got to learn you know, had to do wage scales and all sorts of different — give service to the members and collect the union dues and do the banking. Coming out of a jazz band.
